newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JULY 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JULY 2.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--Inflation is expected to rebound on its downward trend so far this year to increase slightly to 5.6-5.7 percent for the month of June. The increase is due to the prices of seasonal foodstuffs and is expected to continue in July, due to increases in public transport fares and other public services.

--There are important changes in the pipeline for the taxation system, beginning in autumn with the submission of the new budget. The Spraos committee meanwhile is examining how to boost public revenues.

--A new scandal threatens to engulf the Athens Stock Exchange just months after the Delta Securities affair, which is still to be prosecuted. Following the arrest of broker Adam Yiannopoulos on Monday on charges of embezzling 1.5 billion drachmas, there were reports yesterday that another small firm was unable to meet commitments.
--Private investors flocked to subscribe to yesterday's issues of annual T-bills and two-year zero coupons with the finance ministry raising 208 billion drachmas.

--A number of smaller brokerage firms appear to be facing difficulties, with Katsoulis Securities unable to trade yesterday and battling to meet a one billion drachma bill. Contrary to reports, Katsoulis has not 'disappeared' but was locked away in consultations with his staff on the problems yesterday. Sources said at least another two firms would face similar problems.

--The government yesterday presented its prototype for a new model for labour relations for the new century: among the six new measures are the abolition of a rigid eight-hour day, drastic cutbacks in overtime and disincentives for pensioners' employment.

--The finance ministry is bolstering its efforts against tax evasion with two new bills submitted to Parliament yesterday. One of the bills requires all individuals and companies resident in Greece to have a tax identification number (AFM).

--The finance ministry aims to recoup a large part of debts owed to the state - estimated at 1.6 trillion drachmas - by the end of the year and is feverishly at work on compiling lists of those owing more than five million drachmas.
--FTSE International and the Athens Stock Exchange officially introduce a new index on September 24, designed to track the performance of the investible market in Athens.

--Finance ministry and Bank of Greece officials begin negotiations towards the end of the week with representatives of a Japanese banks on taking out a 200 billion drachma Samurai bond loan. The loan would cover 20 percent of planned foreign borrowing, the finance ministry estimates.

--Development Minister Vasso Papandreou hit back at comments directed at her by Intracom president Socrates Kokkalis yesterday, saying the only person she accepted orders from was the prime minister. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
